source.title: Critical Data Size of Language Models from a Grokking Perspective
source.authors: Xuekai Zhu; Yao Fu; Bo-Wen Zhou; Zhou-Han Lin

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neural scaling laws, but its experiments study grokking and data sufficiency in small models trained from scratch; it does not test the claim’s power-law losses, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or related versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites neural scaling laws and contrasts them with its grokking results. Its own relevant results concern classification accuracy and data requirements across model sizes, not held-out pretraining loss or parameter/token/compute power-law fits. The model-size and layer-count findings are recorded as related results under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study induces grokking on purpose (rescaled initialization, weak weight decay) in 1-layer to 6-layer Transformers trained from scratch on classification tasks. It measures classification accuracy and generalization steps against data fraction and hidden size or depth. It fits no power law to held-out pretraining loss, makes no extrapolation, and does no compute-optimal or fixed-parameter shape comparison. Its remarks on scaling laws are discussion only.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that a critical data size marks the shift from memorization to generalization under their grokking configuration, and that this critical size grows with model size. They speculate that normal scaling-law behaviour appears only once data is sufficient. They also note the results hold only in simplified toy settings.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines grokking with small Transformers trained from scratch rather than measuring the original scaling-law recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with model size, layer count, and dataset fraction. The authors also state that their grokking results depend on initialization rescaling and weight decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the induced-grokking configuration on IMDB, average accuracy across data fractions falls as hidden size rises from 16 to 256. More layers need more data to generalize.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small from-scratch classifiers trained with induced grokking, the critical data size for generalization grows with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Some smaller models beat slightly larger ones when data is limited. The authors call this similar to inverse scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With insufficient data for a single task, larger models can underperform smaller ones.

record.problems: The experiments use simplified models and grokking-specific settings; the authors state that reproducing grokking on larger models such as 7B is a challenge. The reported model-size comparisons concern classification accuracy rather than pretraining loss or compute scaling.

untested.parts: All: no held-out pretraining loss fits against parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation from small runs.
All: depth and width are varied without holding parameter count fixed, and the measure is accuracy, not loss.
All: no power-law fits in other regimes.
All: no downstream evaluation of pretrained models scaled up.
All: no exponent fits or fitting-choice comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not one of the original sources. Its scaling-law statements in the Section 5 discussion and Appendix G are interpretive and back no fitted law, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger-run loss from fits on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as compute grows.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count and their effect on loss.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance after pretraining, or its relation to pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices, and bending of fitted power-law curves.

rows.subject: 1-layer encoder-only Transformer
rows.size_stated: Hidden size varied from 16 to 256 in increments of 16
rows.operation_detail: Varied hidden size and evaluated accuracy across dataset fractions.
rows.measure: Average accuracy across all data fractions
rows.value: The average accuracy decreases as hidden size increases.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval shown for the average-accuracy results; numerical interval not stated.
rows.note: The text reports the trend; the result aggregates accuracy across the tested data fractions and hidden sizes.
rows.check: The measure is classification accuracy averaged over data fractions under an induced-grokking configuration, not pretraining loss in parameters, tokens or compute. No version applies. The trend direction is correctly stated.

rows.subject: Transformer models with varying layer counts
rows.size_stated: Number of layers varied from 2 to 6
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of layers and evaluated training curves at different data sizes.

conditions.value: various fractions; exact values for this comparison not stated

rows.measure: Data size needed for effective generalization
rows.value: As the number of layers increases, larger data sizes are needed for effective generalization.
rows.note: The text states the directional result; it does not provide separate numerical outcomes for each layer count.
rows.check: This is a qualitative claim about training curves for 2, 4 and 6 layers, with no numbers. Parameter count is not held fixed, so it cannot bear on V4.

rows.subject: Transformer models of varying hidden sizes
rows.size_stated: Hidden sizes varied from 16 to 256; the specific models in this comparison are not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared performance of smaller and slightly larger models with limited training data.

conditions.value: smaller datasets; exact fraction not stated

rows.value: Some smaller models achieve better performance than slightly larger models when trained with smaller datasets.
rows.note: The paper describes this as an inverse-scaling observation but does not identify the specific model pairs or report their values in the text.
rows.check: Model pairs and values are unspecified, and the result is read from a heatmap (Fig 4A). It is an accuracy-based inverse-scaling observation under an induced grokking setup, so no version applies.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
